name: Adoni-Zedek
title: Canaanite king of Jerusalem
summary: Adoni-Sedek was the Amorite king of Jerusalem at the time when the Israelites entered Canaan under Joshua's leadership. His name means 'my lord is righteousness', and forms a remarkable parallel to Melchizedek, who according to tradition was also king in Salem (Jerusalem). When the Gibeonites made peace with Israel, Adoni-Sedek feared the strategic threat this posed, and formed an alliance with four other Amorite kings to punish Gibeon. In the ensuing battle, God intervened dramatically with hailstones from heaven and caused the sun and moon to stand still, so that the Israelites won a overwhelming victory. Adoni-Sedek and the other kings fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah, but were found, humiliated, and executed by Joshua. His defeat marked the beginning of the Israelite conquest of southern Canaan.

keyEvents.title: Heard about Gibeon's peace treaty with Israel
keyEvents.description: Adoni-Zedek became very afraid when he heard that Gibeon, a large and powerful city with skilled warriors, had made peace with Israel and Joshua. Gibeon's switch to the Israelites posed a serious strategic threat to the Canaanite city-states.

keyEvents.title: Formed a coalition against Gibeon
keyEvents.description: Adoni-Zedek sent word to four other Amorite kings—Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish, and Debír of Eglon—and asked them to help him attack Gibeon because the city had made peace with Israel.

keyEvents.title: The siege of Gibeon
keyEvents.description: The five Amorite kings gathered their forces and marched up against Gibeon to besiege and attack the city. The Gibeonites then sent word to Joshua at Gilgal, asking for immediate help.

keyEvents.title: Defeat at Gibeon and God's Intervention
keyEvents.description: Joshua marched up from Gilgal with his entire army after the Lord had promised him victory. God struck the Amorites with confusion and sent large hailstones from heaven that killed more enemies than the Israelites' swords did. The sun and moon stood still over Gibeon and the Valley of Aijalon until the people had taken vengeance on their foes.

keyEvents.title: Adoni-Zedek Hides in a Cave at Makkedah
keyEvents.description: The five kings, including Adoni-Zedek, fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah. When Joshua learned of this, he ordered large stones to be rolled in front of the cave's entrance to keep them trapped until the battle was over.

keyEvents.title: Execution of the Five Kings
keyEvents.description: After the complete victory, Joshua had the five kings brought out of the cave. He commanded his commanders to place their feet on the kings' necks as a sign of total submission—a well-known symbolic act in the ancient Near East. The kings were then killed and hung on five trees until sunset, when they were taken down and thrown into the cave.

versions.summary: Adoni-Zedek was the king of Jerusalem at the time the Israelites entered Canaan under Joshua's leadership. He formed a coalition with four other Amorite kings to attack Gibeon after the Gibeonites had made peace with Israel. He was defeated by Joshua in the famous battle where God sent hailstones and the sun stood still, and was then executed along with the other kings.
versions.title: Canaanite king of Jerusalem
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'warrior' is somewhat imprecise. Adoni-Zedek was primarily a political leader who organized a military coalition, rather than a warrior himself. 'Coalition leader' or 'military commander' would have been more accurate, but 'warrior' can be defended in a broad sense.; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. There are very interesting linguistic, historical, and theological details connected to Adoni-Zedek that should be covered – including the meaning of his name, the connection to Melchizedek, and archaeological findings related to Jerusalem at this time.; [minor] The summary is good, but could mention the theological significance of Adoni-Zedek's name ('my lord is righteousness') being contrasted with his opposition to God's people, as well as the interesting parallel to Melchizedek, who was also king of Salem/Jerusalem.; [minor] In the event 'The Siege of Gibeon,' verse 5 overlaps with the previous event. Verse 5 concerns how the kings gathered and marched up, while verse 6 deals with the Gibeonites asking Joshua for help. It might be clearer to include only verses 6–7 here to avoid duplication.

footnotes.text: The name Adoni-Zedek (Hebrew: אֲדֹנִי־צֶדֶק) means 'my lord is righteousness' or 'lord of righteousness.' This is strikingly similar to Melchizedek (מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק, 'my king is righteousness'), who according to Gen 14:18 was also king of Salem (Jerusalem). Both names contain the element צֶדֶק (tsedeq, 'righteousness'), which may indicate a tradition linked to righteousness in Jerusalem's royal titles.

Jerusalem (Hebrew: יְרוּשָׁלַיִם) is known from Egyptian Execration Texts from around 1900 BC under the name 'Rusalimum,' and from the Amarna letters (around 1350 BC), where the city's ruler Abdi-Heba wrote to the pharaoh. These letters show that Jerusalem was a city-state king in Canaanite times, confirming the biblical picture of Adoni-Zedek as a local king.

It is worth noting the theological irony that Adoni-Zedek, whose name implies 'righteousness,' fought against God's people and God's plan. In biblical narrative, this underscores that true righteousness lies not in human titles but in obedience to God. His fate contrasts with Melchizedek, who blessed Abraham and became a foreshadowing of Christ's priestly kingship (Ps 110:4; Heb 7).

The five Amorite kings who formed the coalition represented important cities in southern Canaan: Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon. The fact that these specific cities allied themselves shows the strategic threat posed by the Israelites, especially after Gibeon—a large and strategically vital city—switched sides to the enemy. Coalition strategies among Canaanite city-kings are well documented in the Amarna letters.

Joshua's command for the commanders to place their feet on the kings' necks (Josh 10:24) was a symbolic act known from the ancient Near East. Egyptian and Mesopotamian reliefs depict similar scenes where the victor places his foot on the defeated one's neck as a sign of total submission and dominance. This symbol is also used theologically in the Bible (cf. Ps 110:1).
